opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that story has stuck with me for a long time. It's from Andy Grove's book *Only the Paranoid Survive*. In the mid-1980s, Intel was basically a memory company. DRAM was its identity, the thing it was founded on. Then Japanese manufacturers came in with better yields and lower prices, and Intel was losing money and getting squeezed out.

What I love is how Grove describes the moment of clarity. He and Gordon Moore were sitting in an office, pretty gloomy, and Grove asked Moore something like: "If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new CEO, what do you think he would do?" And Moore answered right away: "He would get us out of memories." Grove looked at him and said, "Why shouldn't you and I walk out the door, come back in, and do it ourselves?"

To me that's a really powerful thinking tool. It's a kind of mental reset. When you've been running something for years, you carry sunk costs, emotional attachment, your identity, your past decisions. All of that clouds your judgment. Pretending you're a newcomer with no history lets you see the situation as it actually is, not as you wish it were. The data was already telling them memory was over. They just needed a way to emotionally permit themselves to act on it.

And of course they did. They exited DRAM, bet the company on microprocessors, and that turned out to be one of the best strategic pivots in tech history.

I think about this a lot, honestly, in my own work. As an engineer or a founder, you fall in love with what you built. It's very easy to keep optimizing something that's fundamentally on the wrong trajectory. So every so often I try to ask myself: if I were walking in fresh today, knowing what I know about the market and the technology, would I still choose this direction? If the answer is no, that's a signal you should take seriously, even if it's painful. The hardest part usually isn't knowing what to do. It's having the courage to admit it.

r001.rationale: The response says Grove asked Moore what a new CEO would do if they were replaced, and Moore answered that the CEO would get Intel out of memory.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as the "revolving door" moment. In the mid-eighties, Intel was fundamentally a memory company, and the Japanese manufacturers were out-competing them on price and quality in DRAM. Grove tells this story in Only the Paranoid Survive: he's sitting in his office with Gordon Moore, and he asks, "If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new CEO, what do you think he would do?" And Moore says, without hesitation, "He'd get us out of memories." And Grove says, "Then why don't we walk out the door, come back in, and do it ourselves?"

What I find powerful about that is the mental trick. They weren't lacking information. Everyone at Intel could see the numbers. What they were lacking was permission to let go of their identity. DRAM was the product that made Intel, it was their emotional home, and so every discussion was framed as "how do we save memories" rather than "should we be in memories at all." The thought experiment of imagining an outsider stripped away the sunk cost and the sentimentality. The outsider has no memory of the old glory, so the outsider sees only the strategic reality.

The second thing I admire is that the decision itself was cheap, but the execution was brutal and they committed anyway. Grove describes a year or more of actually winding things down, closing fabs, laying people off, with middle managers still quietly fighting to keep DRAM alive. He calls it a "strategic inflection point," where the fundamentals of the business shift ten-x and you have to change the company or die. He also makes a point I've thought about a lot as a founder: the people at the edges of the organization, salespeople, line engineers, often sense the inflection before leadership does, because they get the cold wind first. Leadership is the last to know, precisely because leadership built the thing.

So when I describe their way of thinking, I'd say it's a combination of radical detachment from your own history, plus the discipline to act on a conclusion you intellectually accept but emotionally hate. It's very easy to say "we should pivot." It's very hard to walk back in through that door and actually be the new CEO of your own company. I think about that framing every time I notice I'm defending something because it's ours rather than because it's right.

r001.rationale: It recounts Grove asking Moore what a new CEO would do if the board replaced them, and Moore answering that the CEO would get Intel out of memories.

Grove asked Moore, essentially, “If we were replaced, what would a new CEO do?” Moore said, “Get out of memories.” Then Grove asked, “Why don’t we walk out the door, come back in, and do it ourselves?” That shift in perspective let them reconsider Intel’s direction without treating its history in DRAM as an obligation to stay there.
